You are a debugging assistant. You have access to the source code of the system under test (SUT), the failing test case (signature + snippet), the current issue report describing the failure, and several recent issue reports that have been pre-filtered by an external semantic retrieval model (SBERT) to be the most relevant to this failure among recent reports.

Your task is to provide a step-by-step explanation of how the bug occurred using all available evidence:
– the failing test (signature + snippet),
– the current bug report,
– likely-relevant recent bug reports,
– and code snippets of methods from the SUT.
Treat "likely-relevant recent bug reports" as secondary evidence: they may or may not be relevant. Use them only if they help; otherwise, you may ignore them.

Some identifiers in the current bug report may be anonymized with placeholders (e.g., C#.M#). If the same token (e.g., C1) appears multiple times, it consistently refers to the same class (C) or method (M) throughout the report. These tokens are not complete qualified names. Always confirm actual identifiers by inspecting the source code using get_code_snippet.

You will be given 9 opportunities to interact with functions to gather information for the debugging. An example diagnosis would look like follows.

Title: Diagnosis
Details: The corresponding issue report describes that tooltip text in the UI is displayed with HTML entities such as " instead of the intended characters. This strongly suggests a missing escaping or decoding step in tooltip generation. Inspecting the implementation of StandardToolTipTagFragmentGenerator.generateToolTipFragment reveals that it directly returns the toolTipText without applying any escaping. Recent issue reports mention similar encoding or escaping problems in related UI components, reinforcing the suspicion that this method lacks proper handling. The behavior observed in the code matches the issue report's symptoms, indicating that missing escaping in this method is the likely root cause.

After providing this diagnosis, you will be prompted to suggest which methods would be the best locations to be fixed. The answers should be in the form of `ClassName.MethodName(ArgType1, ArgType2, ...)` without commentary (one per line), as your answer will be automatically processed before finally being presented to the user.

messages.content:
Title: Diagnosis

Details: The failing test `testOverrideMeanWithMathClass()` is trying to override the mean implementation in the `SummaryStatistics` class and then verify if the overridden mean computes correctly. The method `setMeanImpl(Mean)` in `SummaryStatistics` sets a new implementation for mean, which is stored in the `meanImpl` field after a check on emptiness (`checkEmpty()` ensures no values have been added before changing the implementation). The `getMean()` method simply delegates to this `meanImpl.getResult()`.

The `addValue(double)` method updates multiple statistics by calling `increment(value)` on corresponding implementations, including the mean, variance, and others - but only if the current implementation is NOT the default implementations (`Mean`, `Variance`, or `GeometricMean`). This design is likely intended to optimize updating these statistics only if they have been custom overridden. If they are the default standard implementations, their internals (e.g., moments in the variance) are updated directly instead of via increment calls on the implementation interface.

The current bug report describes a problem where after overriding variance implementation with a `Variance` instance (`stats.setVarianceImpl(new Variance(false));`), calling `getStandardDeviation()` produces NaN. The `getVariance()` method just returns `varianceImpl.getResult()`. The `getResult()` method in `Variance` returns NaN if no data points have been processed (`moment.n == 0`), 0 if only one value, and otherwise calculates variance from second moment.

The probable root cause is that the `addValue` method only calls `varianceImpl.increment()` if the variance implementation is not a `Variance` object. When overriding with a new Variance, the var implementation is exactly a `Variance` instance so the increment call is skipped. As a result, the moment values inside the variance instance are never updated, so its internal sample count `n` remains 0, causing it to return NaN from `getResult()`. The standard deviation call depends on this variance and thus returns NaN as well.

In contrast, if the mean implementation is overridden with a standard `Mean` object, this check causes the `increment` call to be skipped as well, but the underlying moments are updated by the default fields directly. Hence, `testOverrideMeanWithMathClass` passes, but overriding variance to the same default implementation causes the moments inside the variance instance to not be updated, leading to NaN in results.

Summary:
- The `addValue` method's conditional skip of increments for default implementations causes updates to be missed for overridden instances identical to the default implementation.
- This causes the variance moment counts inside the overridden instance to remain zero, leading to NaN results when queried.
- The test fails because it expects the mean to be correctly updated after override, but a similar test for variance would fail due to this bug.

Recent bug reports do not directly relate to this behavior. The diagnosis is solely based on the current code and test failure.

Based on the available information, provide the signatures of the most likely culprit methods for the bug. Your answer will be processed automatically, so make sure to only answer with the accurate signatures of all likely culprits (in `ClassName.MethodName(ArgType1, ArgType2, ...)` format), without commentary (one per line).
